heavyToolPlan.approach: Decode/encode via the image crate's unified API in a Web Worker. JPG/PNG/GIF/BMP/TIFF/ICO all work in pure Rust. WebP: decode+encode via image-webp (pure Rust). AVIF: see image-compressor note (encoding is the heavy/risky part). For ICO multi-resolution output use the ico crate. Batch = loop in the worker, transferable ArrayBuffers back to main thread. Pull this into one 'image' crate module since all sub-tools share decode/encode pipelines.
heavyToolPlan.crate: image (default + tiff + ico + bmp + gif features), image-webp, ico, ravif (AVIF encode), image's avif decode; tiff handled by image's tiff feature

heavyToolPlan.approach: PNG: oxipng compiles to wasm32-unknown-unknown with --no-default-features (drop the 'parallel'/rayon feature; threads unavailable). JPEG: do NOT use mozjpeg-sys — it is a C library that needs Emscripten/wasm32-unknown-emscripten and will not link on wasm32-unknown-unknown; instead use the pure-Rust jpeg-encoder crate (formerly mozjpeg-rs spirit) or image's jpeg encoder with quality control — acceptable quality, slightly larger files than MozJPEG. WebP: image-webp lossy/lossless. AVIF: ravif/rav1e compiles to wasm32-unknown-unknown only with the 'asm' feature OFF and threading off — it works but is very slow and large; gate behind a lazy-loaded module. Show before/after byte sizes from the worker.
heavyToolPlan.crate: oxipng (no-default-features), jpeg-encoder (pure Rust) instead of mozjpeg-sys, image-webp, ravif (asm off, threading off)

heavyToolPlan.approach: image crate's resize with FilterType::Lanczos3 for high quality, or the dedicated fast_image_resize crate (pure Rust, SIMD optional) for much faster batch resizing. Aspect-lock and percent math in JS/Rust. Pure wasm32-unknown-unknown, no C deps.
image crate crop_imm/crop to extract the selected region; interactive selection is a JS/canvas concern, Rust just does the pixel crop given x/y/w/h. Pure Rust.

image crate rotate90/180/270 and flip_horizontal/flip_vertical for raster. Arbitrary-angle rotation via imageproc::geometric_transformations (rotate_about_center) with bilinear interpolation. 'Lossless JPEG rotation' (transforms DCT coefficients without re-encoding) is NOT in a pure-Rust crate — implement multiples of 90 via jpeg-decoder + custom coefficient transform if needed, otherwise fall back to decode/rotate/re-encode and document the slight quality loss. Pure wasm.

img-parts compiles cleanly to wasm32-unknown-unknown; it lets you parse JPEG/PNG/WebP container chunks and drop EXIF/XMP/ICC/IPTC segments WITHOUT re-encoding pixel data (true privacy strip, byte-identical image data). This is the correct crate; keep it as the approach.

Decode with image, then quantize. color_quant (NeuQuant) gives a fixed palette; for better dominant-color results use the kmeans_colors crate (pure Rust) or exoquant. Emit HEX/RGB swatches. All pure wasm.

Resize source with image to standard sizes (16/32/48/64/180/192/512), encode PNGs, and pack multi-resolution favicon.ico with the ico crate. apple-touch-icon is just a 180x180 PNG. HTML link tags are static string templates generated in JS. Pure wasm; shares the image module.

usvg parses and normalizes SVG into a simplified tree, then you re-serialize via usvg's writer — this collapses/normalizes a lot SVGO-style (removes metadata, resolves use, rounds coords). usvg is pure Rust and compiles to wasm32-unknown-unknown (it's part of the resvg project, designed for wasm). Note it normalizes rather than doing every SVGO micro-optimization; for pure markup minification you can pair with a regex/whitespace pass. No network.

resvg + usvg parse the SVG, tiny-skia rasterizes to a pixmap, then encode PNG/JPG/WebP via image. All three crates are pure Rust and explicitly support wasm32-unknown-unknown (resvg ships a wasm demo). Transparent background = leave pixmap alpha. Font handling: bundle fonts via fontdb with embedded bytes since there is no system font access in the browser; document that custom fonts must be supplied. No network.
heavyToolPlan.crate: resvg, usvg, tiny-skia, fontdb (embedded fonts), image (re-encode)

heavyToolPlan.approach: Decode + grayscale + downsample with image, map luminance to a character ramp in Rust, optional ANSI color from sampled RGB. Trivial pure-Rust compute, no extra heavy deps beyond image.

Decode each input with image, run a simple rectangle bin-packing algorithm (implement, or use the crunch / texture_packer crate, both pure Rust) and composite onto one RGBA canvas with image, then emit the packed PNG plus a CSS/JSON coordinate map (string-built in JS/Rust). Pure wasm.
heavyToolPlan.crate: image, texture_packer or crunch (or hand-rolled packer)

heavyToolPlan.approach: Decode both with image; compute per-pixel diff and a perceptual/anti-aliased diff using the dssim or the pixelmatch-rs/image-compare crate (pure Rust ports of pixelmatch). Output a highlighted diff image plus a difference percentage. Slider/side-by-side is pure JS. No C deps.
heavyToolPlan.crate: image, image-compare or a pixelmatch port (dssim for perceptual)

heavyToolPlan.approach: Generate: qrcode crate -> render modules, then composite a logo with image (and bump error-correction to H to survive the overlay). Decode: rqrr (pure Rust QR detector/decoder) + image for input decoding. Both pure wasm32-unknown-unknown. Styling (colors/rounded modules) done while rasterizing.

GIF create/optimize/resize/split/extract-frames: the gif crate (encode/decode) + image for per-frame ops, all pure Rust wasm. gifski produces higher-quality GIFs and DOES compile to wasm (used by squoosh-style tools) but pulls in heavier deps; offer it as a lazy-loaded 'high quality' path. APNG via the apng crate / png crate; animated WebP encode is limited in pure Rust (image-webp animation support is partial) — document partial animated-WebP write support. 'Convert video clips to GIF' needs video decode = belongs to the ffmpeg.wasm media-converter, not pure Rust; cross-link rather than duplicate.
heavyToolPlan.crate: gif, image, gifski (optional, lazy), apng/png; video->GIF deferred to ffmpeg.wasm

heavyToolPlan.approach: This is the one ML tool. Pure Rust ort (ONNX Runtime) only targets wasm32-unknown-emscripten and is experimental — do NOT route this through the Rust/wasm32-unknown-unknown pipeline. The correct 100% client-side approach is to run the U2Net/ISNet ONNX model with onnxruntime-web (WASM/WebGPU backend) OR transformers.js (briaai/RMBG, MODNet) directly in JS in a Web Worker, with the model weights served as a static asset from the same origin (no backend, no API). Rust/image can still do the final alpha compositing/replace-background step. Flag: large model download (5-180MB depending on model); make it explicitly user-initiated.
heavyToolPlan.crate: JS onnxruntime-web or transformers.js (NOT pure-Rust ort); image (Rust) only for compositing

heavyToolPlan.approach: image for loading/compositing; imageproc for drawing primitives; text rendering needs glyph rasterization via ab_glyph + imageproc::drawing (bundle a font, no system fonts in browser). Opacity = alpha blend, tiling = loop. Logo watermark = overlay a decoded PNG with alpha. All pure wasm32-unknown-unknown.
heavyToolPlan.crate: image, imageproc, ab_glyph (font), embedded font bytes

heavyToolPlan.approach: libheif-rs is OUT: it wraps the C libheif/libde265 and needs Emscripten (wasm32-unknown-emscripten + C toolchain), not wasm32-unknown-unknown. Pure-Rust HEIC decode is immature. Two viable client-side paths: (1) Prefer the browser itself — many browsers can decode HEIC via createImageBitmap/; draw to canvas then re-encode with the Rust image module. (2) Bundle a prebuilt libheif compiled to wasm via Emscripten (libheif-js / heic2any / a libheif.wasm) loaded as a static asset in a Worker, then hand RGBA to Rust for JPG/PNG/WebP encode and EXIF handling via img-parts. Either way it stays client-side; just not via the pure-Rust crate. EXIF preserve/strip via img-parts on output.
heavyToolPlan.crate: NOT libheif-rs on wasm32-unknown-unknown; use libheif.wasm (Emscripten, static asset) or browser-native decode; image + img-parts for encode/EXIF

heavyToolPlan.approach: No suitable pure-Rust crate (proposedCrate is empty, correctly). Use ffmpeg.wasm (@ffmpeg/ffmpeg, an Emscripten build of FFmpeg) loaded as static assets and run in a Web Worker — fully offline once downloaded, no backend. Note the core is ~25-30MB and requires cross-origin isolation (COOP/COEP headers) for its multithreaded build, or use the single-threaded core to avoid that. Trim/mute/extract-audio/clip-to-GIF are all ffmpeg command invocations. This is JS-orchestrated, not Rust.

lopdf compiles to wasm32-unknown-unknown (pure Rust). Use Document::load_mem on each input and lopdf's object/page merging (renumber object IDs, concat Kids, fix the page tree). Pure client-side. Share lopdf across all the structural PDF tools.

lopdf: load once, for each output range clone the doc and delete the pages not in range (or build new page tree referencing kept pages), prune unused objects. Pure wasm. Bundle outputs into a ZIP with zip or async_zip (both wasm-friendly).
lopdf: build a new Document containing only selected pages, copying referenced resources/objects. Same machinery as split. Pure wasm.
lopdf: delete_pages() then prune orphaned objects and renumber. Pure wasm32-unknown-unknown.

lopdf handles reorder (rewrite Kids order), rotate (set /Rotate on page dict), delete. Thumbnails for the drag-and-drop UI need rendering — that is the pdfium/pdf.js concern (see pdf-to-images); use pdf.js or pdfium.wasm just for preview thumbnails, lopdf for the actual mutation. Pure wasm for the mutation half.
lopdf: set/normalize the /Rotate entry (mod 360) on selected or all page dicts. No rasterization needed. Pure wasm, trivial.

Object-level wins are pure-Rust with lopdf: deduplicate objects, recompress streams with FlateDecode (flate2/miniz_oxide — wasm-friendly), drop unused objects, compress to object streams. Real size reduction usually needs image downsampling/re-encoding, which requires decoding embedded images: extract image XObjects, re-encode with image/jpeg-encoder, reinsert via lopdf. This avoids pdfium entirely and stays pure wasm32-unknown-unknown. Quality presets = target DPI + JPEG quality. (pdfium-render in proposedCrate is unnecessary for this.)

This needs a full PDF renderer, which pure Rust does not provide robustly. Two client-side options, both no-backend: (1) pdf.js (Mozilla, JS/wasm) render each page to a canvas then encode PNG/JPG — simplest, well-supported, recommend this. (2) pdfium-render: the Rust wrapper compiles to wasm32-unknown-unknown but REQUIRES a separately Emscripten-compiled pdfium.wasm binary (~several MB) loaded as a static asset and bridged via JS glue. Recommend pdf.js for reliability and smaller footprint; ZIP the outputs with zip/async_zip.
heavyToolPlan.crate: pdf.js (recommended) OR pdfium-render + prebuilt pdfium.wasm (Emscripten static asset); zip/async_zip

heavyToolPlan.approach: printpdf compiles to wasm32-unknown-unknown (pure Rust) and is the right choice: place each image as an XObject on a page with chosen size/orientation/margins. pdf-writer is a lower-level pure-Rust alternative if you want tighter control. Decode inputs with image. Pure client-side.

Parse with csv crate (wasm-friendly), lay out a paginated table with printpdf (manual column-width/auto-fit + page breaks; printpdf has no high-level table engine, so implement layout). Bundle a font with printpdf's font embedding (no system fonts). Pure wasm.
lopdf to read/write the Info dictionary (Title/Author/Subject/Keywords/Creator/Producer) and the XMP metadata stream (parse/serialize XMP as XML with quick-xml). Pure wasm32-unknown-unknown.

lopdf does not implement encryption writing fully; implement the standard security handler manually: RC4 (rc4 crate) for legacy, AES-128/256 via the aes + cbc crates (pure Rust, wasm-friendly — explicitly avoid ring). Compute the encryption key per the PDF spec (MD5/SHA-256 via md-5/sha2), set permission flags, encrypt strings/streams, write /Encrypt dict with lopdf. All pure wasm. This is nontrivial but fully client-side.
heavyToolPlan.crate: lopdf, aes, cbc, rc4, md-5, sha2 (NOT ring); rand for IV

heavyToolPlan.approach: Mirror of encrypt: given the password, derive the key (md-5/sha2), decrypt strings/streams (aes/cbc/rc4), and rewrite the document without the /Encrypt dict via lopdf. Pure wasm32-unknown-unknown, no network. Only works when the user supplies the password (no cracking).
heavyToolPlan.crate: lopdf, aes, cbc, rc4, md-5, sha2

heavyToolPlan.approach: lopdf to append a content-stream overlay per page drawing the number text; needs a font — embed a standard font (the 14 base fonts can be referenced by name, simplest) or embed a TTF subset. pdf-writer can help author the overlay content. Position/format/start-value computed in Rust. Pure wasm.

lopdf: add a watermark XObject (text via base-14/embedded font, or an image) to each page's content with a graphics state for opacity (ExtGState /ca), rotation (cm matrix), and tiling (repeat). Image watermark = embed image XObject. Pure wasm32-unknown-unknown.
heavyToolPlan.crate: lopdf, pdf-writer, image (logo watermark), embedded font

heavyToolPlan.approach: pdf-extract is pure Rust and compiles to wasm32-unknown-unknown; it extracts the embedded text layer (text-based PDFs only, no OCR — matches the description). It can be brittle on complex encodings; lopdf-based manual extraction is a fallback. No pdfium needed. Pure client-side.
lopdf: wrap each source page as a Form XObject and place 2/4/N scaled copies onto each new larger page via cm transforms. Pure Rust, pure wasm. No rasterization.

lopdf: set the /CropBox (and optionally /MediaBox) on pages. Manual mode = user rect. Auto-detect-whitespace needs rasterizing pages to find content bounds — either approximate from page content-stream bounding boxes in pure Rust, or render via pdf.js/pdfium for true whitespace detection. Manual crop is pure wasm; auto mode optionally uses the renderer.
lopdf: change /MediaBox dimensions and apply a scaling cm transform to content (or wrap page as XObject and scale onto new A4/Letter page) to preserve aspect ratio. Pure wasm32-unknown-unknown.

lopdf: render each AcroForm field's appearance stream and annotation appearance into the page content stream, then remove the interactive form/annotation objects. Doable in pure Rust but tedious (must handle field appearance generation); fields lacking appearance streams may need generation. Pure wasm; complex. For full fidelity a pdfium-based flatten is more robust but adds the Emscripten pdfium dependency.

lopdf + pdf-writer to add the required pieces: embed all fonts (subset/embed TTFs — the hard part, needs a font subsetter; consider the subsetter / allsorts crate, pure Rust), add an OutputIntent with an ICC profile (embed a bundled sRGB ICC), add the PDF/A XMP metadata (quick-xml), set the document ID. Pure wasm32-unknown-unknown but the most involved tool; true PDF/A validation (veraPDF) cannot run client-side, so present it as best-effort conversion, not certified compliance.
heavyToolPlan.crate: lopdf, pdf-writer, quick-xml, a font subsetter (subsetter/allsorts), bundled sRGB ICC

heavyToolPlan.approach: serde_json + serde_yaml, both pure Rust wasm. Note serde_yaml is archived/unmaintained — prefer serde_yaml_ng or serde_yml (maintained forks) for new work. True comment-aware round-trip requires a CST parser; serde-based conversion loses comments, so either document that, or use the yaml-rust2 / saphyr crate to preserve structure. Pure client-side.
heavyToolPlan.crate: serde_json, serde_yaml_ng or serde_yml (avoid unmaintained serde_yaml); saphyr/yaml-rust2 for comment-aware

heavyToolPlan.approach: serde_json + toml crate (toml is the reference parser, pure Rust, wasm-fine). Use toml_edit if you want to preserve formatting/comments on the TOML side. Map serde Value <-> toml Value. Pure client-side.

serde_json + quick-xml (pure Rust, wasm-friendly) for both directions; quick-xml's serde support or manual event-based conversion handles attribute-vs-text-node mapping and pretty printing. Pure client-side.

serde intermediate model: parse YAML (serde_yaml_ng/serde_yml) into serde_json::Value or toml::Value, serialize to TOML (toml). Watch type/null mismatches (TOML has no null) and surface clear errors. Pure wasm.

Parse with a YAML crate to validate (capturing line/col errors), then re-serialize with normalized indentation. serde_yaml_ng for round-trip, or saphyr/yaml-rust2 for a parser that gives precise error positions. Pure wasm32-unknown-unknown.

calamine reads .xlsx/.xls/.ods fully in-memory and compiles to wasm32-unknown-unknown (pure Rust). Iterate worksheets -> rows, emit JSON via serde_json and CSV via the csv crate. Pure client-side. .xls (old BIFF) is supported by calamine too.
similar crate (pure Rust, wasm-friendly) for line/word/char diffs with Myers/patience algorithms; render side-by-side or inline in JS. Pure client-side.

regex crate compiles to wasm32-unknown-unknown. Note its syntax differs from JS/PCRE (no backreferences/lookaround) — if the tool advertises JS-regex semantics, run it via the browser's native RegExp in JS instead; if it advertises Rust regex, use the crate. fancy-regex (pure Rust) adds lookaround/backrefs if needed. Decide based on which dialect you market. Pure client-side either way.
heavyToolPlan.crate: regex (or fancy-regex for lookaround; or native JS RegExp)

heavyToolPlan.approach: pulldown-cmark (pure Rust, GFM support, wasm-friendly) to render HTML, then sanitize with the ammonia crate (pure Rust HTML sanitizer) to prevent XSS in the preview. Both compile to wasm32-unknown-unknown. Pure client-side.

unicode-normalization for NFC/NFD/NFKC/NFKD (pure Rust wasm). For per-character name/category, unicode_names2 (names) + unicode-general-category or the unicode-properties crate. These embed Unicode data tables (size cost). Pure client-side.

Streaming hashing in a Web Worker: read the File in chunks (Blob.slice/ReadableStream), feed each chunk to update() of sha2 (SHA-256/512), sha1, md-5 (RustCrypto, pure Rust wasm), blake3 (pure Rust, wasm; disable its 'rayon' and platform-asm features for wasm32-unknown-unknown), crc32fast. Avoid ring entirely. Verify-against-expected = constant-time compare. Pure client-side, handles large files via streaming.
heavyToolPlan.crate: sha2, sha1, md-5, blake3 (no rayon/asm), crc32fast

heavyToolPlan.approach: blake3 (XOF output, keyed hashing, derive_key) and sha3 (RustCrypto Keccak/SHA-3, plus SHAKE128/256 XOF) — both pure Rust, compile to wasm32-unknown-unknown. For blake3 turn off rayon/SIMD-asm features on wasm. Pure client-side.

bcrypt crate (RustCrypto, pure Rust, wasm-friendly) for hash with configurable cost and verify. Needs randomness for the salt — use getrandom with the 'js' feature so it pulls entropy from crypto.getRandomValues in the browser. Run in a Worker (high cost factors block). Pure client-side.

argon2 crate (RustCrypto) supports Argon2id/i/d, PHC string output, tunable m/t/p; pure Rust, compiles to wasm32-unknown-unknown. High memory cost is the constraint — run in a Worker and cap memory to what wasm linear memory allows (watch the 32-bit address space / ~2-4GB ceiling; surface OOM gracefully). getrandom(js) for salt. Pure client-side.

rsa crate (RustCrypto, pure Rust) generates 2048/3072/4096-bit keys and exports PEM/DER via pkcs8/pkcs1. Compiles to wasm32-unknown-unknown; needs getrandom('js') for a CSPRNG seed. 4096-bit keygen is slow in wasm — run in a Worker with a progress/spinner. Avoid ring. Pure client-side.

p256/p384 (NIST P-256/P-384), ed25519-dalek (Ed25519), k256 (secp256k1) — all RustCrypto/dalek, pure Rust, wasm-friendly. Export PEM via pkcs8/sec1 and JWK by emitting the coordinates as base64url with serde_json. getrandom('js') for keygen. Avoid ring. Pure client-side.
heavyToolPlan.crate: p256, p384, ed25519-dalek, k256, pkcs8, sec1, getrandom (js)

heavyToolPlan.approach: x509-parser (pure Rust, nom-based) parses DER; use the pem crate to unwrap PEM first. Extract subject/issuer/validity/SANs/key-usage/extensions; compute SHA-1/SHA-256 fingerprints with sha1/sha2. Compiles to wasm32-unknown-unknown. Chain display is just parsing each cert. Pure client-side.
x509-parser includes PKCS#10 CSR parsing (X509CertificationRequest); pem to unwrap. Show subject, public key, requested SANs/attributes. Pure Rust wasm, client-side.

pem crate (parse/encode PEM blocks, expose block type/label) + base64 for re-encoding bodies; der crate for structural validation. All pure Rust, wasm-friendly. Convert by base64-decoding PEM body to DER and vice versa. Pure client-side.

bcrypt crate for bcrypt entries; APR1-MD5 ($apr1$) implement with md-5 (it's a specific iterated-MD5 scheme); SHA entry = sha1 + base64; crypt (DES) via the pwhash crate if needed. All pure Rust wasm. getrandom('js') for salts. Build the username:hash line in Rust. Pure client-side.
heavyToolPlan.crate: bcrypt, md-5, sha1, base64, getrandom (js); optional pwhash for crypt/apr1

heavyToolPlan.approach: ed25519-dalek (Ed25519), rsa (RSA PKCS#1v1.5 / PSS), p256/k256 (ECDSA) — all pure Rust RustCrypto/dalek, wasm-friendly. Load keys via pkcs8/pem, sign/verify with the matching digest (sha2). getrandom('js') for randomized signatures (PSS/ECDSA). Avoid ring. Pure client-side.
heavyToolPlan.crate: ed25519-dalek, rsa, p256, k256, sha2, pkcs8, pem, getrandom (js)

heavyToolPlan.approach: base64 crate (pure Rust, fast, wasm) to encode any uploaded file's bytes (with optional data: URI prefix incl. MIME detection) and decode back to a downloadable Blob. Do it in a Worker for large files. Pure client-side.
No external crate needed (proposedCrate empty, correct) — format bytes into offset/hex/ASCII columns in pure Rust (or even pure JS). Worker-stream for large files. Pure client-side, tiny.
heavyToolPlan.crate: std only (optional: pretty-hex or hexdump crate)

heavyToolPlan.approach: flate2 with the default miniz_oxide backend is pure Rust and compiles to wasm32-unknown-unknown (do NOT enable the zlib/zlib-ng C backend). GzEncoder/GzDecoder with selectable Compression level. Pure client-side. (Browser-native CompressionStream is also an option for gzip/deflate, but flate2 gives level control.)
flate2 (miniz_oxide backend) DeflateEncoder/DeflateDecoder (raw) and ZlibEncoder/ZlibDecoder, with level control. Pure Rust wasm. Pure client-side.
brotli crate (pure Rust, no C) compiles to wasm32-unknown-unknown with quality (0-11) and window-size tuning for both compress and decompress. Pure client-side.

The default zstd crate wraps the C libzstd via zstd-sys and needs a C toolchain/Emscripten — risky on wasm32-unknown-unknown. Better: use the pure-Rust ruzstd for decompression (compiles cleanly to wasm32-unknown-unknown) and the pure-Rust zstd-rs by KillingSpark (the 'zstd' pure-Rust impl, different from the C-binding crate) for compression, OR confirm zstd-sys builds under your wasm C setup. Recommend pure-Rust ruzstd (+ KillingSpark encoder) to stay on wasm32-unknown-unknown with no Emscripten. Pure client-side.
heavyToolPlan.crate: ruzstd (decompress, pure Rust) + KillingSpark pure-Rust zstd encoder; avoid C-binding zstd/zstd-sys on wasm32-unknown-unknown

heavyToolPlan.approach: qrcode crate (pure Rust) generates the matrix; render to SVG (its built-in SVG renderer) or to PNG via image. Logo overlay + colors done while rendering (raise EC level to H). Error-correction selectable. Pure client-side.
heavyToolPlan.crate: qrcode, image (PNG), optional resvg if rasterizing the SVG

heavyToolPlan.approach: Build the WIFI:T:...;S:...;P:...;; payload string in Rust/JS, then encode with the qrcode crate to SVG/PNG. Pure Rust wasm, client-side, trivial.

QR: rqrr (pure Rust detector/decoder, wasm-friendly) on an image decoded via image, or from a camera frame (getUserMedia -> ImageData -> Rust). 1D barcodes: bardecoder is older/limited; for robust client-side 1D+2D consider the JS ZXing-wasm or @zxing/library since pure-Rust 1D decoding is weak. Recommend rqrr for QR (Rust) + ZXing-wasm for general barcodes if needed. Pure client-side.
heavyToolPlan.crate: rqrr (+ image) for QR; ZXing-wasm/zxing-js for general 1D barcodes (bardecoder is limited)

heavyToolPlan.approach: barcoders crate (pure Rust) generates Code128/Code39/EAN-13/UPC-A with checksum handling; it can emit SVG directly and image (PNG via its image feature). Compiles to wasm32-unknown-unknown. Pure client-side.

bip39 crate (pure Rust) generates/validates 12-24 word mnemonics and derives the seed; entropy from getrandom('js'). For BIP32 key derivation add bip32 (pure Rust). Wordlists embed (small size cost). Pure client-side, no network.

rug is OUT for wasm: it wraps GMP/MPFR (C libraries) and does NOT compile to wasm32-unknown-unknown without Emscripten. For arbitrary-precision client-side use pure-Rust bignum crates: dashu (integers+floats+rationals, pure Rust, wasm-friendly) or num-bigint + rust_decimal/bigdecimal. For the expression parser/evaluator use meval, evalexpr, or fasteval (pure Rust). Combine a pure-Rust evaluator with dashu for big-number mode. Pure client-side.
heavyToolPlan.crate: dashu (or num-bigint + bigdecimal) instead of rug; meval/evalexpr/fasteval for parsing

heavyToolPlan.approach: num-prime (pure Rust: primality tests, factorization) + num-bigint for big integers, num-integer for gcd/lcm. All compile to wasm32-unknown-unknown. Heavy factorizations run in a Worker. Pure client-side, no network.

cannotRunClientSide.reason: Listed as 'Currency Converter (offline rates)' in the light tools. Live FX rates are inherently a network resource. The honest client-side approach is to ship a static rates snapshot bundled at build time and clearly label it 'offline rates as of <date>'. Anything claiming live/current rates would require phoning home to an FX API, which violates the no-backend/client-only constraint.
cannotRunClientSide.recommendation: Keep it, but ship bundled static rates with a visible 'rates as of <date>' disclaimer. Do NOT fetch live rates from any API. Optionally let the user paste/import their own rate table. The current 'offline rates' naming already signals this — preserve that.

feasibility.notes:
ARCHITECTURE — crates vs code-splitting: Do NOT ship one giant shared wasm. The crypto/text/data tools (hashes, base64, compress, serde converters, regex, diff) are tiny and could share one small feature-gated crate, but the image, PDF, and ML/media families are large and must be split. Recommended grouping into a handful of feature-gated wasm crates, each lazy-loaded (dynamic import) only when its tool route is opened: (1) core-text-crypto (sha/md/blake3/sha3/hmac/bcrypt/argon2/base*/hex/pem/der/x509/keys/sign — small, can be one crate with cargo features so unused algos tree-shake); (2) compress (flate2/brotli/ruzstd/zip); (3) data-convert (serde_json/yaml/toml/quick-xml/csv/calamine/similar/regex/pulldown-cmark/unicode); (4) image (the big one — image+webp+ravif+oxipng+resvg+imageproc+qrcode+rqrr — feature-gate per tool to keep each tool's slice smaller, this is where wasm bloat lives); (5) pdf (lopdf/printpdf/pdf-writer/pdf-extract); (6) math (dashu/num-*). Per-tool feature gates inside each crate + Worker-side lazy loading gives the code-splitting wins without the maintenance cost of dozens of crates. Rationale: one mega-crate would force every visitor to download AVIF/PDF/Unicode-table bytes for a simple base64 task.

RANDOMNESS: every keygen/salt/IV tool must depend on getrandom with the 'js' feature (or rand + getrandom/js) so entropy comes from crypto.getRandomValues. Without it, getrandom fails to compile/run on wasm32-unknown-unknown.

CRATES TO AVOID on wasm32-unknown-unknown (all are C-backed / need Emscripten): ring (use RustCrypto instead — already the plan), mozjpeg-sys (use jpeg-encoder), oxipng's parallel feature (build no-default-features), libheif-rs (use browser-native HEIC decode or a prebuilt libheif.wasm asset), zstd/zstd-sys C bindings (use ruzstd + KillingSpark pure-Rust encoder), rug (GMP/MPFR — use dashu/num-bigint), pdfium-render's pdfium binary and ort/onnxruntime (both need Emscripten + large prebuilt assets). For ravif/blake3/oxipng remember to disable asm/SIMD-assembly and rayon/threads features for wasm32-unknown-unknown (no threads unless you adopt wasm threads + SharedArrayBuffer + COOP/COEP headers).

THINGS THAT ARE NOT PURE-RUST-WASM BUT STILL 100% CLIENT-SIDE (use prebuilt Emscripten wasm or JS libs as static same-origin assets, never a backend): media-converter (ffmpeg.wasm, ~25-30MB, COOP/COEP for MT build), pdf-to-images / pdf rasterization & thumbnails (pdf.js recommended, or pdfium.wasm), background-remover (onnxruntime-web or transformers.js + a static ONNX model, large download), heic-converter (libheif.wasm or browser-native), qr-barcode-reader general 1D barcodes (zxing-wasm). All stay offline after first load.

LIGHT-TOOL NETWORK SCAN (only one genuine offender): currency-converter is the single light tool whose value implies live data — already flagged above; keep it offline-snapshot only. Two near-misses that are FINE because they operate on user-pasted input and must NOT fetch: opengraph-preview (OpenGraph & Meta Preview) and email-header-analyzer — implement them to parse user-provided HTML/headers only; explicitly do NOT add a 'fetch URL' button (that would require a CORS proxy/backend). har-viewer, user-agent-parser, curl-to-code, json-to-fetch, sitemap-generator, robots-txt-generator, meta-tags-generator all just transform/inspect pasted text and need no network — confirmed client-safe. world-clock/timezone-converter need the IANA tz database: bundle it (chrono-tz / tzdb embedded) rather than querying any time API. Everything else in the light list is pure local computation.

ACCURACY NOTES VERIFIED THIS SESSION: confirmed ort requires wasm32-unknown-emscripten (experimental, not unknown-unknown); pdfium-render needs a separate Emscripten-built pdfium.wasm; oxipng builds for wasm with parallel disabled; ravif/rav1e build for wasm with asm off; mozjpeg-sys and libheif-rs are C and need Emscripten; zstd C-binding needs a C toolchain so pure-Rust ruzstd is the wasm32-unknown-unknown path. serde_yaml is unmaintained/archived — recommend serde_yaml_ng or serde_yml. All RustCrypto hashing/AES/key crates and lopdf/printpdf/pdf-writer/calamine/image/qrcode/flate2/brotli/base64/quick-xml/toml/regex/pulldown-cmark are confirmed wasm32-unknown-unknown compatible."

architecture.decisions:
## Key Decisions / Tradeoffs

1. Build-time codegen over `require.context`/`import.meta.glob`. `import.meta.glob` is Vite-only; `require.context` is hard to keep type-safe and to guarantee per-tool code-splitting. A Bun `Glob` codegen step (`scripts/gen-registry.ts`) emits explicit `import()` statements, so webpack/turbopack produce one lazy chunk per tool, and we get build-time validation (unique id/slug, valid `relatedTools`, valid category). Cost: a generated, gitignored file and a prebuild hook. This is the only mechanism that satisfies "self-registering folders + no central switch + static export + strict types" simultaneously.

2. Static metadata vs lazy bindings split in `ToolMeta`. `ToolMetaStatic` is JSON-serializable and powers the search index, cards, `<meta>`, and `generateStaticParams` with zero JS pulled in. `component`/`loadWorker` are lazy fns so opening a tool is the only thing that downloads its UI + wasm. Tradeoff: two-shape type, but it keeps the home page and per-tool pages tiny.

3. Lazy wasm inside the worker, not the main thread. The `.wasm` is imported via dynamic `import()` inside `worker.ts`, and the worker is only constructed by `loadWorker` when a tool mounts. Result: wasm chunk downloads strictly on demand, never blocks first paint, and never touches the UI thread (no jank). `--target web` async init makes the `.wasm` a normal hashed static asset the SW can cache.

4. Transferables + correlation-id protocol. ArrayBuffers move with a transfer list (zero-copy) rather than structured-clone copies — essential for image/file payloads. A monotonic `id` correlates requests/progress/responses/cancels, enabling concurrent ops and a clean promise+progress API in `useWorkerOp`.

5. Per-domain Rust crates, not per-tool. All image tools share `image-tools` so the `image` crate (and the heavy `image` Rust dependency) compiles once and dedupes in the bundle. Cost: a tool can pull a slightly larger shared wasm than a hyper-minimal per-tool build, but it massively reduces total bytes and build time across a family of tools.

6. PWA offline = SW caches `/_next/static/*` (incl. `.wasm`) + precached routes. Because everything is static and content-hashed, a stale-while-revalidate + precache strategy gives true full-offline. The static export emits `out/tools/<slug>/index.html` per tool, so deep links work offline. Recommend Serwist (Workbox successor, App-Router friendly) over hand-rolled `sw.js`, with `/offline` as navigation fallback.

7. Cross-origin isolation via service worker, not server headers. `output:'export'` means no server to send COOP/COEP, which `wasm-bindgen-rayon` requires. The SW injects those headers on navigations and self-reloads once to gain isolation. Tradeoff: an extra first-load reload and SW complexity, isolated to parallel tools only; single-threaded tools are unaffected. `loadWasm` (+ a `parallel` convention) flags which tools need it.

8. `images.unoptimized:true` and no server features. Required by static export — rules out next/image optimization, ISR, route handlers, middleware, server actions. All dynamic behavior is client-side; SEO relies on prebuilt HTML + `generateMetadata`. Acceptable for a privacy-first tool app where all compute is client-side by design.

9. TS strict end-to-end. The generic `OpMap` threads exact request/response types from each tool's `ops.ts` through `useWorkerOp` and `BatchRunner`, so a wrong payload or mishandled result is a compile error. The codegen file is fully typed (`ToolConfig[]`), so registry consumers are strict too.

10. Client-side zip with fflate. Batch outputs are zipped in-browser (`lib/zip.ts`) — no server round-trip, preserves the privacy guarantee, and works offline. Tradeoff: large batches hold results in memory; mitigated by fflate's streaming API and bounded `concurrency` in the worker pool.

11. Icons as string names, resolved client-side. `icon` is a lucide name string (not a component import) so `ToolMetaStatic` stays serializable and the search index/home grid don't eagerly import an icon module per tool; a single `<Icon name={...}>` resolver maps the string at render time.

Verified locally: Bun 1.4.0, Rust 1.95.0, cargo 1.95.0, and wasm-pack are all installed in this environment, so this stack is build-ready. The repo is an empty git repo (greenfield) — no existing code constrains the design.

- text-xs: 0.75rem / 12px, lh 1rem / 16px (secondary meta, breadcrumb, captions, option labels)
- text-sm: 0.8125rem / 13px, lh 1.25rem / 20px (DEFAULT body/UI — buttons, inputs, card titles, nav)
- text-base: 0.875rem / 14px, lh 1.375rem / 22px (tool descriptions, denser prose)
- text-lg: 1rem / 16px, lh 1.5rem / 24px (section headers, card group titles)
- text-xl: 1.125rem / 18px, lh 1.625rem / 26px (tool page H1)
- text-2xl: 1.375rem / 22px, lh 1.875rem / 30px (homepage hero/lead, rare)
- text-3xl: 1.75rem / 28px, lh 2.125rem / 34px (max — landing only)

MONOSPACE USAGE (the developer-tool soul): every input/output textarea, generated values (UUID/hash/JWT/base64), inline code, numeric stats ("1,204 chars · 312 bytes"), all kbd hints, breadcrumb path segments, tool slugs, byte/char counters, diff views, table cells with data. Mono is tabular-nums everywhere numbers update live (font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums) to prevent layout jitter.
design.spacingLayout:
SPACING — keep Tailwind 4px base but lean on the dense rungs. Default gaps 8/12; section gaps 16/24; page padding 16 (mobile) -> 24 (desktop). Avoid 48/64/80 vertical whitespace blocks (that reads as marketing/AI-slop). Vertical rhythm between dense sections: 24px max.

GRID:
- App max-width: 1440px content, but tool workspace can go edge-to-edge within a 1600px max for wide I/O panes.
- Persistent left sidebar (nav/categories): 240px fixed (collapsible to 56px icon-rail). Sidebar is sticky, full height, its own scroll.
- Main content: 12-col CSS grid, 16px gutter, 24px column gap on lg.
- Homepage category grid: auto-fill minmax(280px, 1fr), 12px gap. Tool cards within: minmax(220px,1fr), 8px gap.
- Tool workspace: 2-col split (input left / output right) at >=1024px using grid-cols-2 gap-4; collapses to stacked grid-cols-1 below. Options bar spans full width above or as a 3rd narrow column (280px) on ultra-wide.

BORDER RADIUS (from --radius: 0.5rem / 8px):
- rounded-sm = calc(radius - 4px) = 4px (badges, kbd, tiny chips)
- rounded-md = calc(radius - 2px) = 6px (buttons, inputs, dropdown items)
- rounded-lg = radius = 8px (cards, panels, popover)
- rounded-xl = calc(radius + 4px) = 12px (command palette, modal, top-level containers)
- Full only for avatars/status dots. NO pill buttons on primary actions — pills read consumer-y; keep 6px.

DENSITY targets: button height 32px (h-8) default, 28px (h-7) sm for toolbars, 36px (h-9) for primary CTA only. Input height 32px. Row height in lists 32-36px. Card internal padding 12-16px (p-3/p-4), never p-6+. Icon size 16px default (size-4), 14px in dense toolbars. Line-height tight; rely on borders/dividers to separate, not whitespace.
design.homepageLayout:
HOMEPAGE — a dense dashboard, NOT a centered hero. Layout top to bottom:

1) PERSISTENT SHELL: left sidebar (240px) with logo + global search trigger ("/" hint), category list with live tool counts as right-aligned mono pills, Favorites/Recent at top, theme toggle + GitHub link pinned at bottom. Top bar (48px, sticky, border-b): breadcrumb-style "All tools", center-stretched command/search input (max-w-xl, NOT centered hero — left-aligned in content), kbd hint "⌘K", and a right cluster (theme, layout density toggle, settings).

2) COMMAND BAR (in-page, not modal): full-width search input row, h-9, mono placeholder "Search 140+ tools… (regex, base64, jwt, uuid)". Below it a horizontal scroll row of filter chips: All · Crypto · Converters · Web · Text · Network · Data — each with count. text-sm, h-7 chips, active = primary-tinted.

3) RECENT / PINNED STRIP (only if user has history): eyebrow label "RECENT", a single horizontal row of compact tool cards (icon chip + name + category dot), h-12, overflow-x scroll. Quietly omitted for new users (no empty-state hero).

4) CATEGORY GRID (the core): sections per category, each = eyebrow header row [category icon chip in cat color][Category name (text-lg/600)][count pill mono][optional "view all" ghost link right]. Under it a responsive grid of TOOL CARDS.

TOOL CARD (dense, the signature element):
- Container: rounded-lg border bg-card, p-3, hover: border-foreground/15 + subtle bg-accent + 2px left inset border in category color (box-shadow inset 2px 0 var(--cat)). transition 120ms.
- Row 1: [icon chip 24px rounded-md, category-color bg @12%, icon @ full hue, size-4] + [tool name text-sm/500 truncate] + [optional star/pin toggle ghost, appears on hover, right].
- Row 2: description text-xs muted-foreground, line-clamp-2.
- Row 3 (meta footer, mono text-2xs muted): category name · maybe "offline" badge (privacy signal) · keyboard hint. Use a tiny green dot for "runs locally / no network".
- Whole card is a link; entire surface clickable; focus-visible ring.
- Grid: grid gap-2, auto-fill minmax(260px,1fr). Tightly packed, many per row.

5) FOOTER: thin, mono, single line — "All processing happens in your browser. No data leaves your device." + version + GitHub. This privacy line is a persistent trust signal, styled understated (text-2xs muted).

No giant illustrations, no gradient blob hero, no "Get Started" CTA. The grid IS the landing.
design.toolPageLayout:
TOOL PAGE — consistent shell (same sidebar + top bar as home). Main column structure:

1) BREADCRUMB (h-8, text-xs mono): Home / [Category] / [Tool] — segments are links, separators "/" in muted-foreground. Category segment colored in its cat-accent. Right side of breadcrumb row: action cluster — [Pin/star ghost btn][Share/permalink][Report issue] all icon-only h-7.

2) HEADER BLOCK (compact, py-3): Row with [category icon chip 28px] + [H1 tool name text-xl/600 tracking-tight] + [tiny "offline" badge]. Below: one-line description text-sm muted-foreground (max-w-2xl). Do NOT center; left-aligned, tight.

3) WORKSPACE (the meat) — a bordered panel, rounded-lg, divided into regions by hairline borders (border, not whitespace):
   - OPTIONS BAR: full-width toolbar across top of panel, h-auto py-2 px-3, bg-muted/40, border-b. Holds the tool's controls — selects, switches, segmented toggles, number inputs — laid out inline-wrap with 8px gaps, each labeled with text-xs label above or inline. Segmented control (Radix ToggleGroup) styled like a tabbed switch for modes (e.g. Encode/Decode).
   - I/O SPLIT: grid grid-cols-2 gap-0 with a center divider (border-r), each pane min-h-[320px].
     * INPUT pane: header row (h-8, px-3, bg-muted/30, border-b) = label "INPUT" eyebrow + utility buttons (Paste, Upload file, Clear, Sample) as h-7 ghost icon+text. Body = mono textarea, resize-y, p-3, text-sm, font-mono, no border (panel provides it), spellcheck off, with line numbers gutter optional for code tools.
     * OUTPUT pane: header "OUTPUT" + buttons (Copy [shows "Copied ✓" 1.5s], Download, Open in…). Body = mono, read-only, selectable; copy uses navigator.clipboard. Errors render inline as a destructive-tinted banner at top of output pane, mono, with the exact error.
   - LIVE STATUS FOOTER of panel: h-7 border-t bg-muted/30 px-3, mono text-2xs muted — live stats: "input: 1,204 chars · 312 bytes · 18 lines  |  output: 428 chars  |  processed in 2ms". tabular-nums. This real-time counter is core to the power-tool feel.
   For multi-step tools (CyberChef-like), allow a vertical "recipe" stack of operation cards instead of single options bar.

4) RELATED TOOLS: eyebrow "RELATED", a row of 3-4 compact tool cards (same dense card, smaller) from same category + by shared tags.

5) ABOUT / NOTES (collapsible, default closed for power users): short explainer, examples, references — in a <Collapsible>, text-base prose, max-w-2xl. Keeps page dense by default but discoverable.

State: all options + input persisted to URL query / localStorage so refresh and share-links restore the workspace. Permalink encodes input (with explicit opt-in for privacy).
design.commandPalette:

design.componentStyle:
SHADCN/UI STYLING (the anti-AI-slop tactics are the point):

GLOBAL: baseColor neutral but overridden with cool-tinted oklch above. radius 0.5rem. Borders are first-class — almost everything has a 1px border; we separate with hairlines, not shadows or whitespace. Shadows are minimal and tight (no big soft glows).

SHADOWS: 
  --shadow-xs: 0 1px 2px 0 oklch(0.2 0.02 264 / 0.04)
  --shadow-sm: 0 1px 3px 0 oklch(0.2 0.02 264 / 0.06), 0 1px 2px -1px oklch(0.2 0.02 264 / 0.06)
  --shadow-md (popover/palette only): 0 4px 12px -2px oklch(0.2 0.02 264 / 0.12), 0 2px 6px -2px oklch(0.2 0.02 264 / 0.08)
  Dark mode: shadows nearly invisible — instead lift via border + bg one step lighter + optional inset 0 0 0 1px white/4%.

BUTTONS (h-8 default, px-3, text-sm, font-medium, rounded-md, gap-2, active:scale-[0.98] subtle):
  - default (primary): bg-primary text-primary-foreground, border border-primary, shadow-xs, hover brightness/opacity-90. Used sparingly — ONE per view.
  - secondary: bg-secondary text-secondary-foreground border-border hover:bg-accent — the workhorse.
  - outline: bg-transparent border-border hover:bg-accent — toolbar buttons.
  - ghost: no bg/border, hover:bg-accent — icon buttons, card actions.
  - destructive: bg-destructive.
  - Sizes: sm h-7 px-2.5 text-xs; icon size-8 (icon-sm size-7).
  - Avoid gradients, glows, full-rounded pills.

INPUTS/TEXTAREA: h-8, rounded-md, border-border, bg-background (light) / bg-muted (dark for subtle inset), text-sm, focus: ring-2 ring-ring/40 + border-ring, placeholder muted-foreground. Tool I/O textareas use font-mono. No heavy inner shadow.

CARDS: rounded-lg border bg-card, shadow-xs (light only), p-3/p-4. Hover interaction via border color + bg-accent, NOT scale or big shadow.

BADGES/KBD: rounded-sm, text-2xs, px-1.5 h-5, mono. kbd = border-border bg-muted with subtle bottom border (border-b-2) for keycap feel.

TABS/TOGGLEGROUP: underline or segmented (bg-muted container, active item bg-background + shadow-xs) — segmented preferred for tool modes.

SELECT/DROPDOWN/POPOVER: rounded-lg, border, shadow-md, p-1, items h-8 rounded-md text-sm, check/leading icons size-4.

TOOLTIP: tiny, rounded-md, bg-foreground text-background (inverse), text-2xs, fast (delay 200ms). Use for icon-only buttons.

ANTI-AI-SLOP TACTICS (concrete):
1) Default to 13px UI + dense spacing — kills the airy generic look instantly.
2) Hairline borders everywhere; structure with lines, not floating cards in whitespace.
3) Mono everywhere data lives — signals "tool", not "marketing site".
4) Single restrained primary color; categories add color only via small accent chips/dots.
5) No centered hero, no gradient blobs, no emoji bullets, no 3-card "features" row, no glassmorphism.
6) Persistent sidebar + top bar app-shell (dashboard, not page).
7) Real-time numeric counters with tabular-nums.
8) Keyboard-first: visible kbd hints, ⌘K, focus-visible rings, "/" to search.
9) Subtle micro-interactions only (120ms, scale 0.98 on press, no bouncy spring).
10) Cool-tinted neutrals (hue ~256-264) instead of pure gray/black — screens, not paper.
11) Tight 600-weight headings (not 700/800), negative tracking on large text.
12) Privacy/offline badges + "runs locally" green dots as authentic functional ornament.
design.aesthetic: A keyboard-first, terminal-adjacent dashboard for builders. The vibe: opening a well-organized engineering tool, not a SaaS landing page. Dense information surfaces bound by hairline borders, cool blue-charcoal neutrals (never pure black/white/gray), and monospace anywhere real data flows — hashes, byte counts, I/O, key hints. One disciplined indigo action color carries every CTA; categories are identified by small saturated accent chips and dots, never flooded backgrounds. The interface is an app shell (sticky sidebar + slim top bar + command palette), measured in 13px UI and 4-8px rhythms, structured by lines instead of whitespace. Every tool page is the same predictable workspace — breadcrumb, tight header, options bar, split mono input/output, live tabular-nums stat footer — so power users build muscle memory. Privacy is part of the look: persistent "runs locally / no data leaves your device" signals and offline badges as honest, functional ornament. The result reads like Linear's density met Raycast's keyboard ergonomics and CyberChef's tool depth: fast, quiet, confident, unmistakably a power tool — the deliberate opposite of centered-hero, gradient-blob AI-slop.
